changelog: Insert a new Core Principle directing the scorer to prefer very-early cuts after initial clause-introducers when safe and to make predicate-ending penalties explicitly conditional on the remainder containing clause-level qualifiers/negation/scope carriers — this addresses the primary finding that a blanket predicate-ending penalty and underweighting of clause-introducers harmed mid-length bins.
findings: The scorer systematically undervalues very-early, dense cuts immediately after clause-introducing particles and initial subordinators (e.g. 'Wenn man', 'Auch wenn', initial adverbials). Those prefixes are often the safest place to cut because they isolate the clause introducer and prevent the left fragment from asserting a claim later reversed or qualified — ask: does the remainder contain an explicit qualification/negation that would reverse the prefix? If not, prefer the early cut.

The prompt applies a blanket penalty to cuts that leave the left fragment ending on a finite verb or 'predicate-ending' prefix. Applied globally, this shifts cuts into names and enumerations and harms mid-length bins. The correct judgement is conditional: penalize predicate-ending prefixes only when the right-hand remainder contains clause-level qualifiers/negation or scope carriers that would change the left fragment's asserted meaning; do not forbid dense cuts inside names/enumerations or short chunks when no such clause-level reversal exists.

diagnosis.why: The new Core Principle (prefer very-early cuts after clause-introducers and make predicate-ending penalties conditional) made the scorer cut earlier around initial clause-introducers, which raised H_set in mid-length bins (≤7 and ≤10) by reducing the previous over-penalization of predicate endings, but caused more harmful very-early splits in short pieces (≤3 and ≤5) that fragment heads/NPs, leaving the overall effect near zero.
diagnosis.lesson: Respect that preferring very-early cuts helps mid-length examples but can hurt very-short pieces by splitting heads/NPs, so later revisions should avoid forcing those very-early cuts in short contexts.
